speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the consultation. I am Dr. Agent. You are presenting with respiratory distress; can you tell me exactly when these symptoms started and were you born prematurely?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born at 33 weeks of gestation. The newborn is presenting with respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy until premature onset of labor. There was no significant prenatal care history mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the history; being born at 33 weeks with distress starting 2 hours after birth is concerning for prematurity-related lung issues. Do you notice any grunting breath sounds, nasal flaring, or chest retractions during his breathing episodes?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Grunting, Intercoastal and subcostal retractions, Peripheral cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of grunting, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and peripheral cyanosis in a 33-week preterm infant shortly after birth is highly suggestive of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS). I need to assess the severity of the hypoxia and lung aeration. REQUEST TEST: Arterial_Blood_Gas; REQUEST TEST: Pulse_Oximetry; REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_X-Ray.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Arterial_Blood_Gas: pH 7.30, PaCO2 50 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L; Chest_X-Ray: Fine reticular granulation with ground glass appearance on both lungs; Pulse_Oximetry: Peripheral cyanosis present (consistent with reduced PaO2).

speaker: Doctor
text:
The arterial blood gas confirms respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia, and the chest X-ray showing a ground-glass appearance with fine reticular granulation is classic for surfactant deficiency. Given the history of prematurity and these specific findings, do you have a family history of severe asthma or other chronic lung diseases?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
